title: Works and Days, Hesiod
subtitle: 8th century BC
subject: litterature
description: Hesiod speaks to his brother Perses: work, be just, beware of excess. Between the myth of Pandora and a farming calendar, an ethic of labor is born.

hero.hook: Before there were books of wisdom, a farmer poet was already lecturing his brother.

blocks.text: Around the **8th century BC**, in [[Boeotia]], a region of central Greece north of Attica, the poet **Hesiod** wrote **Works and Days**. It is not an epic about warrior heroes. It is a poem addressed to his brother **Perses**, accused of cheating him out of the family inheritance with the help of corrupt judges.

Hesiod mixes myth, morality and farming advice. Working the soil, respecting justice, avoiding pride: everyday life becomes poetry. With Homer, his texts lay the foundation of much of Greek mythology and Greek thought.

sections.title: A poet who speaks from his field

blocks.text: Unlike **Homer**, the half-legendary figure of epic poetry, Hesiod puts himself in the picture. He names his village, **Ascra**, in Boeotia, his father who came from Asia Minor, the region of today's Turkey, and his lawsuit against Perses. The **Muse**, goddess of artistic inspiration, chose him, he says. But the tone stays concrete: sow, harvest, sail at the right moment.

blocks.caption: Hesiod: Greek poetry comes down into the fields

blocks.text: This personal voice announces something modern: an author who is involved, not just an anonymous bard. Hesiod speaks from the land, not from the palace or the battlefield. He invents didactic poetry, poetry that teaches.

To explain how hard life is, Hesiod tells the story of **Prometheus**, the Titan who stole fire for humankind, and of **Pandora**, the first woman, whose jar let loose every evil on the world. He adds the [[five ages of mankind]]: gold, silver, bronze, heroes and iron. We live in the **age of iron**, the worst of them, where justice wavers and work is hard.
[[Hesiod's Theogony]], the same poet's other great work, tells how the gods were born out of **Chaos**, the original void. Works and Days moves the other way, from the sky down to the plow.

blocks.caption: Prometheus and fire: in Hesiod, technical progress has a price

blocks.text: The moral heart of the poem sets *Dike*, justice and right order, against [[Hubris]], the excess that makes a man think he is the equal of the gods. Unjust kings are threatened by **Zeus**, king of the gods. The honest farmer still has a chance. Hesiod does not promise paradise. He promises that effort is worth more than fraud.

The **calendar of work** gives the poem its rhythm: when to plow, when to pick the grapes, when to keep away from the sea. Wisdom is seasonal. Knowing the rhythms of nature also means respecting an order larger than the appetite of the moment. Perses is scolded like a lazy brother, not like a king.

sections.title: The ancestor of poems about the land

blocks.text: **Virgil**, the Latin poet of the 1st century BC, remembered it in the [[Georgics]], his didactic poem on farming. Moralists from [[Erasmus]], the Renaissance humanist, down to modern readers have found an ethic of labor in it. Hesiod is not gentle. He is clear: without work and without justice, a community rots.

Hesiod also speaks of the **good Eris**, goddess of useful rivalry, who pushes a neighbor to work harder, against the **bad Eris**, goddess of hatred and lawsuits. In a harsh world that distinction matters: competition is not war. The poem becomes an art of living together, rooted in the seasons and in moderation.
**Works and Days** invents a poetry of everyday farm life. Hesiod tells his brother, and us: cultivate your field, avoid excess, because the age of iron forgives neither laziness nor injustice.
